newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan seen cutting palladium use due to high price.
newsitem.headline: Japan seen cutting palladium use due to high price.

text.p: Japan's electronics industry, concerned over the stability of Russian palladium supplies and rising prices, is stepping up efforts to switch to cheaper substitutes such as nickel, industry sources said on Tuesday.

Most industry sources agreed that Japan's palladium demand from the electronics sector would fall slightly this year from last year, even though output of electronic components has been vigorous so far this year.

The electronics sector mainly uses palladium in the production of tiny components known as multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCC), which are used in a wide variety of electronic and telecommunications equipment, especially cellular phones.
Electronics accounted for about 60 percent of Japan's palladium demand in 1996, according to the latest report by Johnson Matthey Plc, a top palladium refiner.
Japan is the world's top consumer of palladium, and Russia is the largest supplier.

Although electronic components makers have enjoyed strong demand for MLCCs this year, they said tough price competition was forcing them to develop ways that would enable them to use cheaper materials.
"We just can't afford to use such a high-priced metal (palladium) as the condensers market is buyers' market," an official with a leading electronic components maker said.
"All we can do is to step up ongoing efforts to reduce use of palladium in electronic components amid fears over supplies and volatile prices," he said.
"It is inevitable that efforts to substitute nickel will accelerate," he said.

Japan's output of ceramic condensers for the first two months of 1997 rose by 36.8 percent from the same period a year earlier, according to a latest statistics released by Electronic Industries Association of Japan.
An all-out shift to nickel is not expected as palladium is needed to produce MLCCs with only few layers, which are higher in quality, compared to those with numerous layers, industry sources said.
Sources at electronic makers also said they were trying to downsize electronic parts, in order to cut the material cost.
Other uses of palladium, such as medical equipment, dental fillings and catalytic converters for cleaning up car exhausts, are less prone to substitution, industry sources said.
Palladium prices have been on the rise since Russia suspended exports of the metal last December.
Spot palladium rose to 172.00/173.00 per ounce at 0550 GMT Tuesday, the highest level since April 1995.

The key price level at which electronics manufacturers have been said to switch from palladium to cheaper metals has been pegged at about 500 yen to 550 yen per gram including freight on the loco Tokyo spot market, industry sources said.
On Tuesday, palladium was quoted at 667 yen per gram in the loco Tokyo market.

Traders said Russia's platinum group export agency (Almazjuvelirexport) has previously boosted palladium sales from stockpiles whenever prices rose too far, above levels of $160 per ounce, in order to discourage substitution.
However, such selling was not emerging this time, traders said.
"I think Almaz knows that high prices dampen palladium demand, but other bureaucrats in Russia may not understand this fact," an official at a bullion house said.

Some precious metal industry sources said not only political turmoil but also a shift in Russia's policy to keep platinum group metals (PGM) prices high by restricting exports was behind the ongoing suspension in exports.
